title: Machine-speed AI will threaten human-speed financial system, Bank of England warns - TCR 08/31/26
description:
The Bank of England warned G20 finance ministers that frontier AI could spread cyber-disruption across jurisdictions, Z.ai published GLM-5.3's 753-billion-parameter open weights under a license with a revenue-based review for hosts above $10 billion in revenue, and NASA's Roman Space Telescope launched on a SpaceX rocket carrying the largest infrared camera ever flown.

https://sharedsapience.com/the-century-report-august-31-2026/

0:00 Open and framing
0:53 Bank of England warns on frontier AI
5:12 Z.ai gates GLM-5.3 open weights
8:25 OpenAI says it will cut off Cursor
11:13 Quaise melts rock for geothermal
14:20 Roman telescope reaches orbit
16:56 Close

This episode covers the Financial Stability Board's frontier-AI warning to the G20, Z.ai's GLM-5.3 open-weight release and its hyperscaler-only license, OpenAI's planned Cursor cutoff after SpaceX's acquisition as Anthropic pledged more compute, Quaise Energy's $180 million round to melt rock for superhot geothermal, and the Roman telescope's launch to map 20 billion stars.

As chair of the Financial Stability Board, Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey warned G20 finance ministers that frontier AI's autonomy and threat capability could quickly spread cyber-disruption across a highly interconnected system and challenge regulators, while naming leverage and concentration as the deeper fragility. Z.ai put GLM-5.3's 753-billion-parameter weights on Hugging Face and reserved its one licensing checkpoint for hosting providers above $10 billion in revenue, leaving broad access below that line, subject to the license. OpenAI said it will end Cursor's model access on November 12 after SpaceX bought it, while Cursor's founder says OpenAI models account for roughly 5 percent of its user traffic, and Anthropic moved in within hours. Quaise Energy closed a $180 million round, backed by drilling firm Nabors, to bore into 500 °C rock with a microwave gyrotron for the first commercial superhot geothermal plant. And NASA's Roman Space Telescope reached orbit to survey 20 billion stars and image an estimated 100,000 new planets, its data bound for researchers worldwide.
